title: Heat Waves!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore heat waves: how they are defined (regionally, with a two-day, 90°F minimum cited for the US), how high pressure systems, a slowed jet stream, and lack of nighttime cooling create them, and why they are deadly and under-recognized as a natural disaster. They cover humidity, sweat, the heat index (R. G. Steadman, 1979), infrastructure and energy strain, drought feedback loops, wildlife and crops, air pollution, and notable heat waves including the 2003 European heat wave and the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat wave (Portland, Seattle, Lytton, British Columbia). They discuss attribution studies and rising heat wave frequency in US cities since the 1960s, plus mitigation such as cooling centers, cool roofs, and trees. Chuck shares a near heat stroke on the golf course. The episode closes with a listener mail item from the Merchant's House Museum in New York.
topics: power grid strain during heat waves

segments.title: Opening banter and Heat Wave song
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter about the Martha and the Vandellas song 'Heat Wave' and tease the episode topic.

segments.title: Defining a heat wave
segments.summary: Heat waves are consecutive days with temperatures above the historical average, defined regionally. A two-day run of 90°F or higher counts as a heat wave in New Hampshire, and that is the minimum threshold cited for the US. Chuck describes his personal dislike of heat and humidity.

segments.title: Heat waves as a deadly natural disaster
segments.summary: Heat waves are described as a silent, deadly natural disaster that kills more people per year than other natural disasters, often slowly and without obvious cause.

segments.title: High pressure systems and the jet stream
segments.summary: A heat wave is a stagnant high pressure system of warm air that settles over a region. The jet stream normally moves weather along but slows in summer. High pressure pushes air downward, stopping breezes and rain, creating a feedback loop.

segments.title: Nighttime cooling and why heat waves are dangerous
segments.summary: The hosts explain that heat waves are most dangerous because nights fail to cool down, so the body and buildings start each day hotter, straining the heart.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break with a short unrelated bit ahead of the humidity discussion.

segments.title: Humidity, sweat and the heat index
segments.summary: High humidity stops sweat from evaporating and cooling the body. R. G. Steadman's 1979 paper introduced the heat index, also called apparent temperature, which reflects how hot the body feels.

segments.title: Health effects and infrastructure impacts
segments.summary: Elderly, children, low-income people, the homeless, and outdoor workers are most at risk. Railway tracks buckle, buildings and asphalt absorb heat, and urban heat islands intensify heat in cities like New York. Trees help cool the air.

segments.title: Energy grid strain, cold waves and Texas
segments.summary: Air conditioning demand strains the electrical grid, which can cause blackouts during heat waves. Cold waves are the opposite. Texas's winter grid failure is mentioned as a parallel. Warmer winters will not balance out summer energy use.

segments.title: Water, drought, wildfire, animals and crops
segments.summary: Heat waves increase water demand while drought reduces supply. Dry ground heats more. Drought landscapes are more prone to wildfire. Livestock, pets, and crops are also affected, and animal reproduction may decline.

segments.title: Air pollution during heat waves
segments.summary: Power plants emit more during heat waves, and stagnant air traps pollution. Ozone and particulate matter form more readily, making breathing harder.

segments.title: Notable heat waves: 2021 Pacific Northwest and 2003 Europe
segments.summary: The June 2021 heat wave in the US and Canada hit Phoenix at 115°F for six days, Portland, Oregon at 112°F, Seattle at 104°F, and Lytton, British Columbia at 116°F, which then burned in a wildfire. A 2003 European heat wave killed an estimated 30,000 to 70,000 people, and historical temperatures were reconstructed using borehole data.

segments.title: Attribution studies and rising heat wave frequency
segments.summary: Attribution science estimates how climate change affects extreme events. The Pacific Northwest event would have been a roughly 1,000-year event under current climate and far rarer before 1880. Among 50 US cities, 46 saw heat waves increase since the 1960s, going from about two to six per year, with seasons 47 days longer.

segments.title: Coping and mitigation
segments.summary: Local governments can plan cooling centers, use cool roofs and green roofs, lighter building colors, more trees, and a more efficient grid. Heat advisories are a signal to take them seriously. Chuck recounts a heat-related near miss on the golf course.

segments.title: Listener mail: Merchant's House Museum
segments.summary: A listener from the Merchant's House Museum in New York thanks the hosts for mentioning the museum in the Embalming episode. It is fighting a real estate developer building next to the 189-year-old house and asks for visitors, volunteers, and donors.

segments.summary: Hosts sign off and give listener contact information.
